reason: Every card this generation was random origin and every one drew from the same correlated sector pool, so the trait tilts the deterministic pass reported rest on a field too thin to distinguish a pattern from a draw. Widening the sampled field before the lane commits to a direction costs one generation of compute and buys the ability to tell whether the long-hold, loose-stop shape is actually the lane's edge or just the card that happened to win a small draw. This is the change I would make instead of touching the margin or the window split.

With a wider draw, carrying a slightly larger elite keeps the next generation's parents from collapsing into a single design with variations, which is the risk when the top of a narrow field is dominated by one discipline. It also gives the mid-pack volatility card -- the one whose out-of-sample behaviour did not track its selection ranking -- a route into breeding that a median-only elite selection would otherwise close off.

The field was drawn entirely at random and the standings turned out to be close to a straight function of a single trait, which means several draws were near-duplicates in shape and the weight space is barely sampled. Raising the number of cards per generation is the cheap purchase at this stage: there is no parent worth exploiting yet, and each additional card costs only a backtest. This is the change to make before any change to the gate -- a wider field is precisely what would let a genuine separation appear above the margin on its own, without redefining what counts as separation.

Elite selection runs on median alone, and this generation produced the exact failure that invites: a card outside the elite cut held up out of sample better than its selection standing suggested, while a card ranked above it did not. Widening the carry-forward slightly, in proportion to the larger draw count proposed alongside it, keeps that kind of card in the gene pool without weakening the ranking rule itself. It is a hedge against median-only elitism, not a replacement for the ranking, and it does not let holdout results back into selection -- the elites are still chosen on selection median, there are simply a few more of them.

This is the amendment the generation actually argues for. The owner's goal has two clauses -- survive a drawdown, keep the trend -- and ranking on the median of selection windows can only see the second one. The evidence is in the standings' own ordering: the card with the least damaging worst window and a perfect window record placed third, while a card whose worst window was among the deepest placed second, and the selection ordering and the holdout ordering disagree with each other. Ranking on the worst window instead makes the selection criterion match the first clause of the stated goal, and it changes what gets bred rather than merely what gets reported. The risk is the mirror image -- a worst-window ranking will favour cards that sit out the market, as one card in this field already shows -- which is why I am pairing this with a larger population and a wider universe direction rather than proposing it alone. If a generation under this ranking produces only cards that avoid participating, that is a clean signal to move to a blended criterion, and it will be visible immediately.

Every card here was random-origin and the field converged on nearly the same universe, so the generation tested fewer genuinely distinct ideas than its size suggests. A larger population is worth spending specifically because the next generation needs to carry three things at once: children of the cards worth keeping, a chop-focused sub-family that this generation barely represented, and cards reaching outside the software-and-semicap pool. At the current size those three compete for the same slots and the chop family loses. This is a widening of coverage, not a change to any threshold.

Scaled alongside the larger population so the elite fraction stays roughly where it is rather than narrowing. There is a second reason specific to this generation: the elite set is what the trait-mean findings are computed against, and with the current narrow elite the reported trait directions are drawn from a handful of cards that mostly share a universe, which makes those directions read as discoveries when they may just be the field's more aggressive cards catching trending windows. A wider elite makes those trait signals worth more.

The whole field drew from one correlated pool of large-cap software and semiconductor-capital-equipment names, so the discipline labels attached to these cards do not correspond to different exposures -- they are the same book with different trait settings. Under a goal about surviving drawdowns, that pool is close to the worst case: those names fall together. Adding defensive sectors, a broad-market and a value wrapper, small caps, and duration and metal gives the next generation a way to express drawdown survival through what it holds rather than only through when it exits. This is a direction for the designer to draw from, not a restriction on the existing names.

This generation spent a substantial share of its slots on cards that were design-identical in everything that mattered, to the point that two pairs returned indistinguishable results and one pair returned identical results outright. Widening the population is not a request for more of the same; it is the space needed to run the distinct experiments the post-mortem names, namely varying the ballast mix, sweeping the growth-sleeve weight, and testing dividend growth alongside a bond leg rather than instead of it, without those experiments crowding out the incumbent family. If the enlarged field again fills with near-duplicates, the fault is in the mutation operator's step size and should be addressed there rather than by adding slots again.

Paired with the wider population so the elite fraction stays close to where it is now. The intent of the population change is to buy breadth of exploration, and holding the fraction roughly constant is what keeps it from silently becoming a loosening of selection pressure instead. Leaving the elite count untouched while the population grows would do exactly that, so this amendment is a correction to the other one rather than a change of policy in its own right.

The owner asked for a sleeve that survives a drawdown without giving up the trend, and selection is currently ranking on the median alone, which is structurally silent about the drawdown half of that sentence. The consequence showed up concretely this generation: the card with by far the shallowest worst window and the lightest turnover in the field was ranked near the bottom and would have been discarded by elite selection, while the cards actually competing at the top were separated by margins the noise floor says are not real. Ranking on the worst window makes selection answer the question that was asked. I want the risk recorded plainly, because it is serious: ranking on the worst window alone rewards a sleeve that survives by never participating, which is precisely how that shallow-drawdown card failed. The check is the field's composition, not its score. If the next generation fills with flat, low-turnover cards that have surrendered the trend, revert this rather than tune it, and consider instead giving the designer an explicit drawdown constraint while leaving the ranking on the median.
